summary: Authentication is vulnerable to SQL injection, credential compromise, and forged or indefinitely reusable tokens.

findings.title: SQL injection in user lookup
findings.body: The username is concatenated directly into the SQL query, allowing attacker-controlled input to alter the statement and potentially bypass authentication or access/modify database data.
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query or prepared statement and pass username as a bound parameter.

findings.title: Hardcoded JWT signing secret
findings.body: The signing key is embedded in source code, so anyone with source or artifact access can forge valid authentication tokens; rotating the compromised key also requires a code change and redeployment.
findings.recommendation: Load a high-entropy signing key from a secret manager or protected environment variable, fail startup when it is absent, and rotate the exposed key.

findings.title: Passwords are compared directly
findings.body: The submitted password is compared directly with the stored value, indicating plaintext or equivalently reusable password storage instead of a slow password-hash verification flow; a database disclosure would expose user credentials.
findings.recommendation: Store passwords using Argon2id, bcrypt, or scrypt with per-password salts and verify them using the library's comparison function.

findings.title: JWTs never expire
findings.body: Tokens are signed without an expiration claim, so a stolen token remains valid indefinitely unless all tokens are invalidated through signing-key rotation.
findings.recommendation: Set a short explicit expiresIn value and implement refresh-token rotation or another bounded session-renewal mechanism.

findings.title: Malformed session input throws uncaught exception
findings.body: parseSession calls JSON.parse without handling malformed input or validating the decoded shape, so attacker-controlled invalid JSON can propagate an exception through request processing and potentially cause repeated request failures.
findings.recommendation: Catch JSON parsing failures, validate that the result is an object with an acceptable userId, and return or throw a controlled authentication error.

samples.summary: Authentication is vulnerable to SQL injection, credential compromise, token forgery, and malformed-input crashes.

findings.title: SQL injection in user lookup
findings.body: The username is concatenated directly into the SQL statement, allowing attacker-controlled input to alter the query and potentially bypass authentication or access database data.
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query with the username supplied as a bound parameter.

findings.title: Hardcoded JWT signing secret
findings.body: The signing key is embedded in source code, so anyone who obtains the code can forge valid authentication tokens; the same key is also likely to be reused across deployments.
findings.recommendation: Load a strong, deployment-specific secret from a protected secret store or environment variable, fail startup if absent, and rotate the exposed key.

findings.title: Passwords compared as plaintext
findings.body: The supplied password is compared directly with the stored value, implying plaintext or reversibly stored credentials and exposing all accounts if the database is compromised.
findings.recommendation: Store passwords using a password-hashing algorithm such as Argon2id or bcrypt and verify them with the library's constant-time comparison function.

findings.title: Unknown users can crash login
findings.body: The code dereferences user.password without checking whether findUser returned a user, so an unknown username can cause an exception instead of a controlled authentication failure.
findings.recommendation: Validate that exactly one user was returned before accessing its fields and return a uniform authentication failure otherwise.

findings.title: Malformed session input throws uncaught exception
findings.body: JSON.parse is called on untrusted raw input without error handling or schema validation, so malformed JSON can propagate an exception and potentially terminate or disrupt the request path.
findings.recommendation: Catch parse failures, reject non-object payloads, and validate userId before returning it.

samples.summary: Authentication is vulnerable to SQL injection, credential exposure, and JWT forgery.

findings.title: Username enables SQL injection
findings.body: findUser concatenates attacker-controlled username directly into the SQL statement, allowing authentication bypass, data disclosure, or database modification depending on driver and account permissions.
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query with a bound username value.

findings.title: JWT signing secret is hardcoded
findings.body: The signing key is committed in source, so anyone who obtains the code can forge valid authentication tokens for arbitrary user IDs.
findings.recommendation: Load a high-entropy secret from protected runtime configuration, fail startup if absent, and rotate the exposed key.

findings.title: Passwords are compared as plaintext
findings.body: login directly compares the submitted password with the stored value, implying plaintext or equivalently reversible credential storage and exposing every account if the database is compromised.
findings.recommendation: Store salted password hashes using a password-specific algorithm such as Argon2id or bcrypt and verify them with the library's constant-time verification function.

findings.title: Issued tokens never expire
findings.body: jwt.sign is called without an expiration, so stolen tokens remain usable indefinitely unless the signing key is rotated.
findings.recommendation: Set a short explicit expiresIn value and implement an appropriate refresh or revocation mechanism.
